function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m happy to walk you through what you’d normally do, but I don’t have the ability to actually clone a repository, inspect its files, or push commits back to GitHub from here. ---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you prefer HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Generate Artifacts

### 2.1 Create/Update a Dockerfile

Inspect the repo first:

```bash
# Look at the package.json to see dependencies and start script
cat package.json
```

If the repo already has a `Dockerfile`, open it and decide whether it needs updating. A typical minimal Dockerfile for a Node.js app looks like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files and install deps
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

If you want to generate this automatically using the helper function (assuming you’re running this inside a Python environment that has the `functions` module available), you could do something like:

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    base_image="node:18-alpine",
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint='["npm", "start"]'
)
```

> **Note:** The helper expects a JSON‑style dictionary; adjust the `entrypoint` format accordingly.

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes Deployment & Service YAML

A simple deployment that runs two replicas of the container and exposes it as a ClusterIP service might look like this:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

If you’d rather generate this via the helper function:

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name="nodejs-welcome",
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome-deployment",
    image_name="your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=2,
    port=3000,
    service_type="ClusterIP"
)
```

> **Tip:** Replace `your-docker-registry` with the actual registry you’ll push to (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow to Build & Push

Create a file `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Important:**  
> * Ensure you have the `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (it’s automatically added by GitHub).  
> * If you’re using a different registry (e.g., Docker Hub), change the login action and tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Add All Changed Files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you generated files via the helper functions, they’ll already be in the correct directories.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Recap of What You Need to Do Manually

| Step | Command |
|------|---------|
| Clone repo | `git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git && cd nodejs-welcome` |
| Inspect `package.json` | `cat package.json` |
| Create Dockerfile | Either write manually or run the helper function |
| Create K8s YAML | Either write manually or run the helper function |
| Create GitHub Actions workflow | Write `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` |
| Stage files | `git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml` |
| Commit | `git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, CI workflow"` |
| Push | `git push origin main` |

Once you’ve pushed, GitHub Actions will automatically trigger the workflow on the next push to `main`. You can verify the build status in the “Actions” tab of the repository.
